newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU summit wrestles over budget deficit limits.
newsitem.headline: EU summit wrestles over budget deficit limits.

text.p: European Union leaders, with financial markets watching them warily, grappled on Friday over how much leeway to give members countries of a single European currency to run up big budget deficits.

After a morning of talks that followed an 11-hour finance ministers' negotiating session, an EU summit failed in its first attempt to agree on a pact for budget discipline when economic and monetary union (EMU) begins in 1999.
"It is a pretty tough fight, and that's an understatement," Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky told reporters.

Germany, whose citizens are wary of giving up the hard deutschemark for the untried euro, stuck to its demands for tighter rules defining when countries that joined the euro could be exempted from fines for overspending.

Diplomats said Bonn was demanding that budget sinners be subjected to automatic fines for running a deficit of more than three percent of gross domestic product unless their economy contracted by at least one percent in a year.
France and Spain argued that the EU's council of ministers must make a political judgment before any fines and sought a lower threshold for exemptions of a 0.75 percent recession.
"It's tough bargaining. It's not just a qustion of the figures," Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen commented.
But diplomats said Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, chairing the two-day summit, was optimistic a deal could be wrapped up later on Friday on the so-called stability pact.
The leaders formally confirmed Dutch central bank governor Wim Duisenberg as head of the European Monetary Institute (EMI) from next July, succeeding Belgian Alexandre Lamfalussy.

But French President Jacques Chirac, reflecting sour Franco-Dutch relations, said that did not mean Duisenberg would automatically head the future European central bank, which will control monetary policy for the euro.
Symbolically, the EMI unveiled the first euro banknotes in Dublin on Friday, giving millions of Europeans a first glimpse of the currency that will enter their pockets in 2002.

The European Commission launched a publicity campaign to ease public acceptance of the new currency earlier this week, unveiling a dollar-style symbol -- a "c" with two horizantal dashes through it -- which it is to represent the euro.

EU sources said Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn warned his colleagues during the night that failure to agree on a stability pact could hurt prospects for the introduction of the euro and give heart to those who sought to prevent it happening.
Financial markets seemed satisfied with the emerging deal but were looking for a quick endorsement from the EU leaders.

While ministers haggled behind the scenes on the final wording of the stability pact, the leaders endured a lecture by British Prime Minister John Major on how they should copy Britain's sweeping labour market deregulation to create jobs.
"Nobody reacted," said one minister at the meeting. "It was a monologue. There was no dialogue."

The growing sense of inevitability about the single currency, despite the stability pact wrangle, could make this an uncomfortable summit for Major, whose Conservative government, torn over European policy, lost its parliamentary majority on Thursday when the opposition Labour party won a by-election.
Facing a general election by May, Major is under strong pressure from Eurosceptics in his party to end his wait-and-see approach to monetary union and rule out joining the euro.

The British leader will also be seeking to resist any move towards closer European integration on the summit's other main agenda item -- a drive to reform EU institutions in preparation for admitting former communist central European countries from around the year 2000.

The Irish presidency of the EU has produced a report to increase cooperation in foreign, defence, interior and justice affairs but it has left aside for now the issue of greater majority voting most sensitive to Britain.
"I don't think it's going to be a summit in which serious decisions are going to be taken," Major told reporters.

France and Germany put forward their own proposals for greater integration on Monday, saying it was vital to give the slow-moving negotiations new momentum if a substantial reform is to be achieved by the deadline of next June in Amsterdam.
